overview.intro: Directed writing asks you to write for a defined reader in a defined form, and the marks sit in the fit between the two. A proposal is read by a committee that wants options and costs; a report is read by an authority that wants findings and recommendations; a speech is heard, so it must be speakable; an article addresses a public and may carry a personal voice; a letter obeys conventions its recipient expects. This chapter takes each form in turn — its layout, its register, its required sections — and then shows how the same material is reshaped when the audience changes. The examinable skill is adaptation: nothing in the answer may suit a different reader than the one named in the question.

facts.label: Brief first
facts.value: The prompt names audience, purpose and form; every mark depends on matching all three.

facts.label: Five forms
facts.value: Proposal, report, speech, article and letter — formal and informal.

facts.label: Layout counts
facts.value: Headings, salutations and sign-offs are part of the answer, not decoration.

facts.label: Exam weight
facts.value: Directed writing is a standing section of Paper 1 with its own mark allocation.

learningOutcomes: Identify the audience, purpose and register a directed-writing task demands.
Write a proposal with options, merits, drawbacks and a recommendation.
Write a report with findings organised under headings and a set of recommendations.
Write speeches and articles that suit a listening or reading public.
Write formal and informal letters with the correct layout, salutation and sign-off.

learn.title: Audience, purpose and register: reading the brief

blocks.text: Every directed-writing task is a contract with a named reader, and the first minute of the answer belongs to reading that contract. The prompt tells you who will read the piece, why they will read it and in what form; a mark is available simply for matching all three, and marks are lost whenever the answer suits a different reader. Register follows audience: a letter to a friend may contract forms and use the first person freely, while a proposal to a committee must use the impersonal third person or a courteous first person plural, avoid slang and state reasons before preferences. Purpose decides structure: an audience that wants to decide needs options and a recommendation, while an audience that wants to know needs findings first. Adaptation is therefore the examinable skill — the same underlying material must be reshaped when the audience changes, and a piece that ignores its brief cannot be rescued by accurate language.

items: Underline the audience, the purpose and the form before writing anything.
Register: impersonal and courteous for official readers; warm and direct for friends.
A decision-making audience needs options and a recommendation; a general audience needs interest.
Sign conventions: Yours faithfully with Dear Sir, Yours sincerely with a named reader.
Layout is answer content: headings, date lines and sign-offs are all marked.

items.text: Brief: “Write to your principal proposing changes to the recess timetable.”
items.note: Audience: an authority. Form: formal letter or proposal. Register: courteous, impersonal, reasons before preference, concrete timings.

items.text: Brief: “Write a speech for younger students on reading for pleasure.”
items.note: Audience: listeners aged eleven to fourteen. Form: speech. Register: warm, direct, short sentences, an address to you and a rhetorical question.

learn.title: Proposals and reports for official readers

blocks.text: The proposal and the report are the two forms an official reader most often requests, and they differ in what the reader is prepared to do. A proposal invites a decision: it opens with the aim, sets out two or three options, gives the merits and drawbacks of each, and closes with a recommendation and, where appropriate, a cost or timetable. Its tone is persuasive but impersonal, because the reader wants reasons rather than enthusiasm. A report records what was found: it opens with the terms of reference, states the method briefly, gives findings under headings and closes with numbered recommendations that follow logically from those findings. Neither form tolerates a personal anecdote as evidence, and neither should bury its recommendation; the examiner looks for the recommendation and counts the headings.

items: Proposal shape: aim, options, merits and drawbacks, recommendation with cost or timing.
Report shape: terms of reference, method, findings under headings, numbered recommendations.
Impersonal voice throughout; reasons stated before preferences.
Recommendations must follow from the findings — a recommendation with no finding loses logic marks.
Headings are content: they show the examiner the structure at a glance.

items.text: Proposal recommendation: “Of the three options, staggered recess best fits the constraints: it costs nothing, requires no staffing change, and reduces the queue length by an estimated third.”
items.note: Three reasons, one decision — the shape an examiner can award.

items.text: Report finding to recommendation: “Finding 3: the library is unused after 2 pm. Recommendation 3: extend the reading club to that hour, monitored for one term.”
items.note: Each recommendation is traceable to the finding it answers.

items.meaning: The statement of what a report covers and who commissioned it.
The weighing of each proposal against merits, drawbacks and cost.
A voice avoiding personal preference, using one, it or the committee.
The action the writer advises, justified by the reasons already given.

blocks.text: Three forms address a public rather than a committee, and each has a characteristic texture. A speech is written to be heard: it opens by greeting the audience, states its point within three sentences because listeners cannot reread, uses short sentences, repeats its key phrase three times for the rhetorical rule of three, and closes with a call to action or a memorable cadence. An article is written to be read: it may open with an anecdote or a striking fact, develops a personal voice, uses subheadings when it is long, and can carry a controlled turn of argument. A letter obeys conventions its recipient recognises: the date, the address, the salutation, the body and the sign-off, with Yours faithfully after Dear Sir or Madam and Yours sincerely after a named reader. Informal letters relax the layout but not the courtesy; formal letters keep the conventions even when the content is friendly.

items: Speech: greet, state the point at once, short sentences, rule of three, memorable close.
Article: hook, personal voice, controlled argument, subheadings if long.
Formal letter: date, address, salutation, body, Yours faithfully or sincerely as required.
Informal letter: relaxed layout, warm register, courtesy retained.
Repetition of a key phrase three times is rhetorical, not careless — vary what surrounds it.

items.text: Speech opening: “Good morning. You have five subjects, three hours of daylight and one attention. I am here to argue that reading for pleasure is how you get it back.”
items.note: Greeting, point and stake arrive in three sentences, speakable at listening speed.

items.text: Sign-off error: “Yours faithfully, R. Sharma” after “Dear Mrs Sharma”.
items.note: A named reader requires Yours sincerely; the mismatch is a convention mark lost.

blocks.caption: Speech techniques that earn marks
rows: sounds formulaic if all sentences match
“And what did we do with it?”
ties the close to the open

learn.title: Reshaping one event for three audiences

blocks.text: The highest-level skill in directed writing is reshaping: taking one set of facts and rebuilding it for a different reader, and the way to practise it is to write the same event three times. Take a concrete incident — a flooded school ground, a failed event, a successful drive for books — and write it as a report for the management, a speech for the assembly and a letter home. The facts do not change; what changes is the entry point, the voice and the density of detail. The report gives the finding and the remedy; the speech gives the shared experience and the call; the letter gives the personal colour and the feeling. Writing all three in one sitting trains the adaptation the examiner is really marking, and it also reveals which details are load-bearing: the facts that survive all three reshapes are the facts the answer cannot do without.

items: Write one event as report, speech and letter to feel what adaptation changes.
Facts stay fixed; entry point, voice and detail density change.
The report leads with the finding, the speech with the shared stake, the letter with the scene.
Details that survive every reshape are the load-bearing facts of the event.
Practise the reshape under time; adaptation is a timed skill, not a leisurely one.

items.text: Incident: the annual sports day rained out.
items.note: Report: findings and a contingency recommendation. Speech: disappointment named, courage rallied, next date announced. Letter: the walk home in wet kit, the smell of the pavilion, the parent who waited.
Report: totals and storage plan. Speech: thanks and the rule of three. Letter: the first box opened, the children’s faces.

items.meaning: Reshaping fixed material so it suits a new audience, purpose and form.
The speech close naming what the audience should do next.
A deliberate return to the opening image or phrase in the close.
The stated audience, purpose and form the answer must satisfy.

keyPoints: Underline audience, purpose and form before writing; each controls a different decision.
Register follows audience: impersonal for officials, warm and direct for friends.
Proposals weigh options and close with a recommendation; reports give findings then numbered recommendations.
Speeches are written to be heard: short sentences, rule of three, memorable close.
Articles open with a hook and may carry a controlled personal voice.
Formal letters keep layout conventions; sign-off follows the salutation.
Headings, date lines and sign-offs are answer content and are marked.
Recommendations must follow logically from the findings that precede them.
Adaptation is the examinable skill: reshape the same facts for each new reader.
Practise one event as report, speech and letter in a single sitting.
examFocus: The examiner searches for the required sections — make them findable with headings.
A proposal without a recommendation, or a report without findings, loses its core marks.
Sign-off mismatches are convention marks lost for nothing: Yours faithfully with Dear Sir.
Speeches must sound speakable; read the opening lines under your breath before submitting.

vocabulary.meaning: The stated audience, purpose and form a directed answer must satisfy.
The level and tone of formality chosen for the particular reader.
A persuasive official document weighing options and recommending one.
The statement of a report’s scope, purpose and commissioner.
The advised action, justified by reasons or findings already given.
An official voice avoiding personal preference and slang.
The speech close that names what the audience should do next.
A deliberate return to the opening image or phrase in the closing lines.

questions.prompt: A letter to the principal requesting a library extension should close with:
questions.explanation: A letter beginning Dear Sir or Madam takes the formal sign-off Yours faithfully.

questions.prompt: Which sentence belongs in the recommendation section of a report?
options: I personally feel the club is a wonderful idea.
Recommendation 2: extend the reading club to the unfilled 2 pm hour, reviewed after one term.
The findings make the situation appear rather serious.
The club has my personal support and admiration.
questions.answer: Recommendation 2: extend the reading club to the unfilled 2 pm hour, reviewed after one term.
questions.explanation: Reports stay impersonal and number recommendations traceable to findings; the first sentence is personal opinion in the wrong register.

questions.prompt: The opening three sentences of a speech should:
options: Thank the chief guest at length
State the point while the audience is still listening closely
Apologise for the weather before continuing
questions.answer: State the point while the audience is still listening closely
questions.explanation: Listeners cannot reread, so the point must arrive while attention on the opening is highest.

questions.prompt: When the same flooded-ground incident is written for three forms, what must never change?
questions.explanation: Adaptation reshapes entry point, voice and detail density — the underlying facts stay fixed.

questions.prompt: A proposal weighs its options and closes with a __________ .
questions.explanation: The recommendation is the proposal’s decision point; the reader is being asked to choose.

questions.prompt: The opening section of a report stating its scope and who commissioned it is called the terms of __________ .
questions.explanation: Terms of reference fix what the report covers and for whom it was written.

questions.prompt: Explain why a personal anecdote is usually unsuitable as evidence inside a report.
questions.answer: A report is read by an official audience that wants findings traceable to a stated method, and a personal anecdote is neither systematic nor checkable, so it weakens rather than supports the finding. The impersonal register of the form also excludes I-based evidence: the reader is evaluating the situation, not the writer’s experience. Where an individual case genuinely illustrates a pattern, it should be reframed as a recorded instance — “one of the twelve cases reviewed” — so that it belongs to the method rather than to the writer.
questions.explanation: Official readers can check findings against a stated method, but they cannot check a writer’s experience.

questions.prompt: Give two reasons the rule of three works in a speech and one risk of overusing it.
questions.answer: First, three items match the rhythm listeners expect, so the claim is easier to hold in mind after hearing it once. Second, a triad can build — rising in intensity or narrowing to the specific — which gives the sentence a designed shape the ear recognises. The risk is formulaic texture: when every sentence is a triad, the pattern stops signalling emphasis and begins to sound like a template, which costs the spontaneity mark the speech form rewards.
questions.explanation: Triads match the rhythm listeners remember, while constant triads turn rhetoric into a visible template.

questions.prompt: Your school’s annual day was cancelled because the hall roof leaked during heavy rain. Write a report to the principal proposing arrangements for the postponed event. Include terms of reference, findings, and at least three numbered recommendations.
questions.answer: Report: Postponement of the Annual Day, 14 October. Terms of reference: to record the circumstances of the cancellation and propose arrangements for the postponed programme, submitted to the Principal by the cultural committee. Findings, under three headings. F1: the hall roof admitted water above the stage during the rain of 12 October; the damp reached the electrical panel, and the district safety officer advised against use. F2: the programme had been rehearsed and the printed tickets carry the original date, so both cast and audience need re-briefing. F3: the next free weekend in the school calendar is 4 November, and the catering and sound contractors have confirmed availability on that date. Numbered recommendations. R1: reschedule the annual day to the evening of 4 November, subject to a safety re-inspection of the hall on 1 November. R2: issue a re-ticketing notice through class teachers within three days, and reprint tickets only if the inspection fails. R3: commission a temporary covered walkway between the gate and the auditorium, since the November forecast shows intermittent showers. R4: hold one full dress rehearsal on 3 November in the hall once the inspection clears it. Each recommendation follows from a finding, and the impersonal register suits the official reader.
questions.explanation: Terms of reference, headed findings and recommendations traceable to them are the marked skeleton of the report.

questions.prompt: A candidate writes a speech for younger students on reading for pleasure that opens with two minutes of thanks to the headmistress and the organisers. Identify the fault and describe how the answer should be restructured to raise its marks.
questions.answer: The fault is structural: the thanks consume the opening in which the speech must state its point, and listeners judge a speech’s stake within its first sentences, so attention allocated to protocol is attention taken from persuasion. The content mark for relevance suffers because the audience named in the brief is younger students, not the dignitaries. The restructure is to compress the acknowledgement to one courteous clause — “Thank you, Mrs Iyer, and good morning to all of you” — and spend the freed sentences stating the point and its stake. The speech should then follow the listening shape: a short anecdote about a first book, the claim that reading for pleasure builds attention, the rule-of-three triad of benefits, one direct address to the students’ own experience, and a call to action naming a concrete first step such as twenty minutes before sleep. A callback to the opening anecdote in the close would give the speech the designed ending the mark scheme rewards.
questions.explanation: A speech must state its stake in its first sentences, because attention spent on protocol is never recovered.
